hints_cache: This is a counting and combinatorics problem in disguise. Since every palindrome is perfectly symmetrical, you only need to figure out the first half of the string; the second half is automatically determined as a mirror image.

Try building the first half of the string one character at a time, from left to right. At each position, you need to decide which letter ('a', 'b', 'c'...) belongs there to reach the k-th lexicographical position.

For any character you consider placing at the current index, calculate how many ways the remaining characters can be arranged using the multinomial coefficient formula. This tells you if the k-th permutation falls within the group starting with that character.

Because k is relatively small (10^6), you can avoid overflow from giant factorials. If your permutation count ever exceeds k, you can simply cap it at k + 1 because you already know you've found the right 'branch' to explore.

Maintain a frequency map of the characters available for the first half. For each index, iterate 'a' through 'z', calculate the permutations of the remaining pool, and if k is larger than that count, subtract the count from k and try the next character; otherwise, place that character and repeat for the next index.
